title: Lantern and the Runaway Cheese
markdown:
The house had that deep hush that arrives when the stars have only just remembered to come out. Moonlight lay on the rug like spilled milk. Lily slept with a whisper of breath, one hand open as if she had been holding a thought and set it down. In the friendly stain of the night-light, Lantern opened his clever eyes and shook his whiskers into working order. He was a rat who was fluffier than his job required and better at the job than his fluff suggested. Beside him Aurelia stirred, pearly, maned like a waterfall that had learned manners. She believed, with a sincerity that could be tiring, that her thoughts improved rooms.

Tiny-bell music came through the slightly open window, shy as a breeze that had practised in the lane. Aurelia’s silver-tipped ears turned. “Lantern. That pretty music.”

Lantern used few words and liked a plan. He nodded. “Music. And maybe laughing.”

She sat up; light ran the spiral of her horn and made the night-light look like a rehearsal. “A party. Or sprites with standards. We must go. I shall see it properly. My way of seeing will make it more wonderful.”

He sighed a puff that barely moved the air. “It is the middle of the night. We are a unicorn and a pet rat. No plan is a kind of plan, and a bad one.”

“Danger is only a chance to be clever,” she said, already rising with the ease of someone who had never filled in a form. “The night smells of sleeping flowers. Come.” She was a dark shape against the stars. Lantern squeaked once, pictured Lily’s peaceful face, and followed into the cool garden, because leaving her alone with a mystery felt worse than following.

They landed on damp grass at the garden’s edge. Silver birches waited beyond the quiet lane, a friendly mystery with a lane-shaped door. The air was moss, wet earth, and those flowers that refuse the day. Moonlight through leaves laid moving maps on the forest floor, light and shadow changing their minds every few steps. They had just entered a small glade that thought well of itself when a gruff official voice stopped them as neatly as a gate.

“Halt. Who, and why?”

A stout hedgehog blocked the path, spines arranged as if order were a grooming choice. He peered with small serious eyes; his nose worked suspicion. “Reason for nocturnal transit. Nighttime travel forms. Section B, Subsection 3. Unannounced arrivals and departures on these paths.”

“A pleasant stroll,” Aurelia said, aiming for calm and important, hoping importance might count as a stamp.

“A stroll.” He puffed until the spines stood straighter. “No permit. No stamped plan. Completely unacceptable. I am Mr. Pricklewick, Head of Nighttime Order and Rules for this area. Rules are how a forest stays polite.”

“We are not applying for a tea party,” Aurelia said, a spark of amusement she did not quite hide.

He bristled until he hummed. “A robin collecting dew needs rules. A thrush after worms needs rules. Mess is what happens otherwise. You see.” He produced a sigh you could hear, a small collapse of patience. “Respect for proper ways is in decline. It is sad, if one is honest, which I am, professionally.”

Even annoyed, he was still a hedgehog in a path, and Aurelia eased them past with her shoulder. Pricklewick trotted after, muttering about paperwork, foundations, and how the forest was coming apart at the edges. The path took them deeper. Streamers appeared between branches, fluttering like quiet flags. This was not just any wood. It kept a calendar, and tonight the calendar had colour.

The music thickened, a cheerful tune that seemed to know where it was going, and led them to a wide moonlit clearing. Homemade lanterns warmed the air. Badgers stood like furniture that had opinions. Owls watched from a height that implied wisdom. Shy rabbits lined the moss. A fox pretended, not very well, not to be a fox. At the centre a wheel of golden cheese was being lowered, with great care, onto a velvet cushion by a badger wearing a garland of sweet-smelling flowers. The cheese looked ceremonial and edible in equal measure.

“The Great Cheese Ceremony,” Aurelia whispered, wonder leaking through her polish. “They really do love it.”

Lantern watched the way people watch a thing that is meant to be shared: the cushion, the faces, the way no one was eating yet because waiting was part of the point. Pricklewick tried, and failed, to press a thick stack of papers on the Cheese Keeper. “Esteemed keeper. Moisture levels. Sub-clause 7, paragraph C. The right dampness is not a matter of taste.”

A playful gust — a squirrel’s joke from a high branch, perhaps — swept the clearing and caught the edge of the velvet. The wheel wobbled, tipped, and rolled, a golden decision picking up speed toward a dark hollow at the clearing’s edge. The hollow looked as if it could swallow a ceremony and not send a receipt. The gasp that went up was communal, one sound from many throats.

The cheese became a blur. Aurelia froze. Her horn offered only an uncertain gleam. “Oh.” Lantern felt the old weight in his chest, the quiet courage that made him move when moving was the useful thing. Pricklewick wrung his paws. “A clear and terrible mistake in the Cheese Protection Rules. Complete chaos. I did warn—”

Elegance, Aurelia discovered in that tilted second, did not chase. Her hooves were for beauty. Fancy sentences had no traction on moss. This was not a problem of grace. It was a problem of speed and a very important wheel.

“We have to,” Lantern said, sharp enough to cut the silence. He saw the hollow, dark and ready. He remembered Lily’s cellar floor, cool stone, how fast a rat could be when a crumb rolled under the shelf. “It will be gone.”

Aurelia blinked; the spark that came back was work, not performance. “How? My hooves are too large for a careful job. My ideas are… insufficient. I am afraid they are not enough.”

Lantern’s eye found a fallen branch near the clearing’s rim, its curve leading almost to the hollow, bark still sound. “The branch. A slide. If I steer.” He did not wait for her to agree or for Pricklewick to announce an emergency protocol. He ran with a speed he had not known he was keeping. He darted in front of the wheel and nudged with all the strength a small body saves for emergencies, aiming the gold at the wood.

The cheese took the branch, wobbled, and slowed enough to be an opportunity instead of a disaster. Lantern scrambled onto the bark, paws a blur, nudging, guiding, talking to the cheese in the wordless language of urgency. Aurelia lowered her head. With a horn-nudge that surprised her by being useful, she eased the last inches off the branch and onto the soft moss at the hollow’s lip. The wheel stopped as if it had meant to all along, a guest who had only been looking for the right chair.

Relief went through the clearing like weather. The garlanded badger came to Lantern, who was panting, fur wrong, spirit unnecessarily bright. “Incredible speed. Never seen anything like it. Brave. Clever.”

Pricklewick held a tiny plastic-covered card in shaking paws. “Well. Highly unusual, of course. Prevented a total ceremonial loss. Acceptable, I suppose. The wind’s intentions should still be investigated. Naturally. I will want statements.”

Aurelia’s pride had thinned to something she could stand in. “That was brave. And smart. I was less help than I had budgeted for. Elegance is a poor brake against runaway cheese.” She nudged him with her nose, ordinary friendship, no swirl. “You saved it. The ceremony too.”

“It needed doing,” Lantern said. “Different strengths.”

The badger rumbled a laugh that settled the remaining nerves. “The music? Young Pip the squirrel, trying to lure the fox closer before the procession. He thought a happy tune might make shyness forget itself. Earnest. A little loud in the execution.”

Aurelia and Lantern looked at each other. A kind mistake, then; not a trick. Kinder than the plot she had invented on the windowsill, and messier than Pricklewick’s subsections.

Dawn put pale rose on the east. They walked back through birches that had gone quiet except for the first birds testing their voices. Pine and wet earth, a comforting used smell after so much official cheese. Aurelia’s steps came down a notch, more companion than procession; her horn caught the growing light and did not show off about it. The moon, already a ghost, laid one last silver strip on the path. Behind them the cheese sat on its moss, unofficial and safe, waiting for a cushion that had learned humility. Pricklewick, somewhere, was already drafting an amendment about wind. Lantern did not need to name what the night had been. He kept pace, and she let him, and the window received them before the house had quite decided to be morning.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
